'''Tityrinæ''' (tit-i-rī′nē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Tityra'' + ''-inæ''.] One of six subfamilies into which the ''Cotingidæ'' have been divided, typified by the genus ''Tityra'', and characterized by the extremely short second primary of the adult males.
{{smaller block|The tarsi are pycnaspidean, and the bill is strong and shrike-like; the plumage is not generally bright, and the sexes as a rule are differently colored. There are 3 genera and about 25 species, two or three of which reach the Mexican border of the United States. The range of the subfamily is nearly coextensive with that of the family.}}

'''Tiu''', ''n.'' A form of ''Tiw''.

'''tiver''' (tiv′ėr), ''n.'' [< ME. *''tever'' (found in an early manuscript as ''teapor'', an error for *''teafor''), < AS. ''teafor'', red, purple.] A kind of ocher which is used for marking sheep in some parts of England.

'''tiver''' (tiv′ėr), ''v. t.'' [< ME. *''teveren'', < AS. ''teofrian'', ''tyfrian'', mark in red or purple, < ''teafor'', red, purple: see ''tiver'', ''n.''] To mark with tiver, as sheep.

'''Tivoli yam.''' See ''yam''.

'''tivy''' (tiv′i), ''adv.'' [Appar. imitative of lively pattering motion. Cf. ''tantivy''.] With great speed: a huntsman's word or cry.
{{smaller block|In a bright moon-shine while winds whistle loud,
''Tivy, tivy, tivy'', we mount and we fly.
{{right|''Dryden'', Tyrannic Love, iv. 1.}}}}

¶
'''Tiw''' (tē′ö), ''n.'' [See ''Tuesday.''] The original supreme divinity of the ancient Teutonic mythology, corresponding with ''Dyu'' of India, ''Zeus'' of Greece, and ''Jove'' of the Romans.

'''tiza''' (tē′zä̤), ''n.'' [Peruv.] The mineral ulexite: so called in Peru.

'''Tizri''', ''n.'' See ''Tishri.''

'''tizwin''' (tiz′win), ''n.'' [Amer. Ind.] Among the Apaches and kindred Indians, an intoxicating distilled liquor similar to the Mexican mescal, said to be made from the yucca or Spanish-bayonet.

'''tizzy''' (tiz′i), ''n.''; pl. ''tizzies'' (-iz). [Corruption of ''tester''<sup>3</sup>.] A sixpence. [Slang.]
{{smaller block|There 's an old 'oman at the lodge, who will show you all that 's worth seeing . . . for a ''tizzy.''
{{right|''Bulwer'', Caxtons, v. 1.}}}}

'''T-joint''' (tē′joint), ''n.'' A joint made by uniting two pieces rectangularly to each other so as to form a semblance of the letter T.

'''Tl.''' The chemical symbol of the metal thallium.

'''tmema''' (tmē′mä), ''n.''; pl. ''tmemata'' (-mạ-tä̤). [< Gr. τμῆμα, a part cut off, a segment, < τέμνειν, ταμεῖν (perf. τέτμηκα), cut: see ''tome''<sup>1</sup>.] A part cut off; a section; a division.

'''tmesis''' (tmē′sis), ''n.'' [< L. ''tmesis'', < Gr. τμῆσις, a cutting, tmesis, < τέμνειν, ταμεῖν, cut: see ''tmema.''] In ''gram.'', a figure by which a compound word is separated into two parts, and one or more words are inserted between them: as, "of whom ''be'' thou ''ware'' also" (2 Tim. iv. 15), for "of whom ''beware'' thou also." Also called ''diacope.''

{{RunningHeader|Tityra|6359|to}}'''Tityra''' (tit′i-rä̤), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. τιτύρας, also τίτυρος, a kind of bird; cf. τατύρας, τέταρος, the pheasant.] A genus of cotingine birds of the warmer parts of America, representative of the ''Tityrinæ''. {{smaller|They are characterized by the unbristled rictus of the strong compressed bill, the slender simitar-shaped second primary of the adult male, and the black and white plumage, which is not very dissimilar in the opposite sexes. Five species range from southern Mexico to southern Brazil, ''T. cayana'', ''T. brasiliensis'', ''T. semifasciata'' (or ''personata'', which reaches Mexico), ''T. inquisitor'', and ''T. albitorques'' (whose Mexican variety is ''fraseri''). Also called ''Psaris'', ''Erator'', and ''Exetastes''.}} '''tityre†''' (tit′i-re), ''n.'' [Also ''tittery'', ''tittyrie''; abbr. of ''tityre-tu''.] 1. Same as ''tityre-tu''. {{smaller block|No news of Navies burnt at seas;
No noise of late spawn'd ''Tittyries''. {{right|''Herrick'', A New Year's Gift Sent to Sir Simeon Steward.}}}} 2. Gin. ''Bailey'', 1731. {{smaller block|Gin . . . sold under the names of double geneva, royal geneva, celestial geneva, ''tittery'' . . . gained . . . universal applause. {{right|''G. Smith'', Complete Distiller, quoted in S. Dowell's Taxes [in England, IV. 103.}}}} '''tityre-tu†''' (tit″i-re-tū′), ''n.'' [So called in some fanciful allusion to the first line of the first eclogue of Virgil: "''Tityre, tu'' patulæ recubans sub tegmine fagi."] One of a band of roisterers or street-ruffians in London in the seventeenth century, similar to the Mohawks, Hawcubites, Hectors, etc. Also spelled ''tittery-tu''. {{smaller block|For the dyet of some of the noble science, some for roaring boyes, and rough-hewd ''tittery-tues''. {{right|''John Taylor'', Works (1630). (''Nares''.)}}}} {{smaller block|Some of the ''Tityre-tu's'', not long after the appearance of this drama (1624), appear to have been brought before the Council, and committed on a suspicion of state delinquency. {{right|''Gifford'', Note on Dekker and Ford's Sun's Darling, i. 1.}}}} '''Tityrinæ''' (tit-i-rī′nē), ''n. pl.'' Also called ''diacope.'' '''to'''1 (tö), ''prep.'', ''adv.'', and ''conj.'' [< ME. ''to'', < AS. ''tō'' = OS. ''tō'', ''te'' = OFries. ''tō'', ''te'', ''ti'' = MD. D. ''toe'' = MLG. ''tō'', ''tū'', ''tē'', LG. ''to'' = OHG. ''zuo'', ''zua'', ''zō'', MHG. ''zuo'', ''zu'', G. ''zu'', to; not in Scand., where ''til'' is used (see ''till''2), or in Goth., where ''du'' is used (the supposed connection of ''du'' and ''to'' is not made out); = OIr. ''do'' = W. ''di'', later ''ddi'', W. ''i'', as a prefix ''dy-'' = Corn. ''dhi'', to; cf. Lith. ''da-'', = L. ''-do'' = Gr. -δε = Zend ''-da'', a demonstrative formative.] '''I.''' ''prep.'' A word used to express the relation of direction or tendency, with many modified and related senses. '''1.''' In the direction of; unto; toward: indicating direction or motion toward a place, point, goal, state, condition, or position, or toward something to be done or to be treated: opposed to ''from''. {{smaller block|From every shires ende Of Engelond ''to'' Caunterbury they wende. {{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 16.}}}} {{smaller block|Be-hold [look] ''to'' thi souereyn in the face with they eyene. {{right|''Booke of Precedence'' (E. E. T. S., extra ser.), i. 58.}}}} {{smaller block|Adonis hied him ''to'' the chase. {{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|Me longeth sore ''to'' Bernysdale, I may not be therfro. {{right|''Lytell Geste of Robyn Hode'' (Child's Ballads, V. 121).}}}} {{smaller block|Thou shalt ''to'' the Mall with us. {{right|''Congreve'', Way of the World, i. 9.}}}} {{smaller block|The natural disposition ''to'' any particular art, science, profession, or trade is very much to be consulted in the care of youth. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 157.}}}} {{smaller block|The General has fallen ''to'' one side in his large chair, whose arms support him from falling to the floor. {{right|''W. M. Baker'', New Timothy, p. 260.}}}} '''2.''' As far as: indicating a point or limit reached or to be reached in space, time, or degree; expressing extent of continuance, or proceeding, or degree of comprehension, or inclusion. {{smaller block|The sun in his sercle set vnto rest, And the day ouer-drogh ''to'' the derke night. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 10735.}}}} {{smaller block|This Tower is easily to be seene ''to'' Milan in a cleare day. {{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 137.}}}} {{smaller block|That which most exasperated the Silures was a report of certaine words cast out by the Emperor, that he would root them out ''to'' the verie name. {{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., ii.}}}} {{smaller block|Sir Tomkyn, drawing his sword, swore he was hers ''to'' the last drop of his blood. {{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, xi.}}}} {{smaller block|And ever James was bending low, ''To'' his white jennet's saddlebow. {{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., v. 21.}}}} {{smaller block|He might have cogitated ''to'' all eternity without arriving at a result. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Social Statics, p. 23.}}}} '''3.''' For; unto: indicating an actual or supposed limit to movement or action, or denoting destination, design, purpose, or aim: as, the horse is broken ''to'' saddle or harness. {{smaller block|The souldiar preparynge hym selfe ''to'' the fielde Leaues not at home his sworde and his shielde. {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 339.}}}} {{smaller block|Wherefore was I ''to'' this keen mockery born? {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., ii. 2. 123.}}}} {{smaller block|They must be dieted, as horses ''to'' a race. {{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 196.}}}} {{smaller block|But ''to'' nobler sights Michael from Adam's eyes the film removed. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 412.}}}} {{smaller block|I shall give Tom an eddication an' put him ''to'' a business. {{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, i. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|He was born ''to'' a large fortune, and had married a lady of the house of Noailles. {{right|''The Century'', XLI. 368.}}}} {{smaller block|If the field is planted ''to'' some other crop, the young lice mature on the grass-roots. {{right|''Amer. Nat.'', December, 1889, p. 1105.}}}} '''4.''' Unto: indicating a result or effect produced; denoting a consequence or end: as, he was flattered ''to'' his ruin; it was reported ''to'' her shame. {{smaller block|I shall laugh myself ''to'' death. ''Shak.'', Tempest, ii. 2. 158.}} {{smaller block|If any man in Englande should goe aboughte . . . to examine yor. life ''to'' yor. utter undoinge. {{right|Quoted in ''H. Hall's'' Society in Elizabethan Age, viii.}}}} {{smaller block|I must not leave this fellow; I will torment him ''to'' madness. ''Beau. and Fl.'', Woman-Hater, ii. 1.}} {{smaller block|The moment the master put his horse ''to'' speed, his troops scattered in all directions. ''Irving'', Granada, p. 94.}} {{smaller block|Then unto them I turned me, and I spake, And I began: "Thine agonies, Francesca, Sad and compassionate ''to'' weeping make me." {{right|''Longfellow'', tr. of Dante's Inferno, v. 117.}}}} '''5.''' Upon; besides: denoting addition, contribution, or possession. {{smaller block|His breath and beauty set Gloss on the rose, smell ''to'' the violet. {{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 936.}}}} {{smaller block|I have a thousand faces to deceive, And, ''to'' those, twice as many tongues to flatter. {{right|''Fletcher and Shirley'', Night-Walker, i. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|Wisdom he has, and ''to'' his wisdom courage, Temper ''to'' that, and unto all success. {{right|''Sir J. Denham'', The Sophy. (''Latham.'')}}}} '''6.''' Upon; on: denoting contact, junction, or union. {{smaller block|Lean ''to'' no poste whils that ye stande present Byfore your lorde. ''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 4. Let me infold thee, And hold thee ''to'' my heart. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, i. 4. 32.}}}} {{smaller block|Then doe they sew a long and black thong ''to'' that thick hide or skin. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 195.}}}} {{smaller block|When all night long a cloud clings ''to'' the hill. {{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}} 7. Compared with: denoting comparison, proportion, or measure. {{smaller|Hence it is used in a strictly limited sense in expressing ratios or proportions: as, three is ''to'' twelve as four is ''to'' sixteen.}} {{smaller block|There is no music ''to'' a Christian's knell. {{right|''Marlowe'', Jew of Malta, iv. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|No, there were no man on the earth ''to'' Thomas, If I durst trust him. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man in his Humour, iii. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|Name you any one thing that your citizen's wife comes short of ''to'' your lady. {{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Westward Ho, i. 1.}}}} 8. Against; over against: denoting opposition, contrast, or antithesis: as, to wager three ''to'' one; they engaged hand ''to'' hand. {{smaller block|He sets the lesse by the greater, or the greater ''to'' the lesse, the equall ''to'' his equall, and by such confronting of them together driues out the true ods that is betwixt them. {{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 197.}}}} {{smaller block|For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face ''to'' face. {{right|1 Cor. xiii. 12.}}}} {{smaller block|My hat ''to'' a halfpenny, Pompey proves the best worthy. {{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 563.}}}} {{smaller block|Tho that they were nine ''to'' ane, They caused [them] take the chace. {{right|''Battle of Balrinnes'' (Child's Ballads, VII. 229).}}}} {{smaller block|Why will you fight against so sweet a passion, And steel your heart ''to'' such a world of charms? {{right|''Addison'', Cato, i. 6.}}}} {{smaller block|A sharp conflict, hand ''to'' hand and man ''to'' man, took place on the battlements. {{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 54.}}}} 9. In accordance, congruity, or harmony with: denoting agreement, adaptation, or adjustment: as, a plan drawn ''to'' scale; painted ''to'' the life. {{smaller block|Ihesu, thou kan me sone amende;
Thou has me made ''to'' thi lyknes. {{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 105.}}}} {{smaller block|And whan ye knowe what it is, loke ye, performe it ''to'' his plesier. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 58.}}}} {{smaller block|His horses and his men
Suited in satin ''to'' their master's colours. {{right|''Peele'', Polyhymnia (ed. Bullen).}}}} {{smaller block|Fashion your demeanour ''to'' my looks. {{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., ii. 2. 33.}}}} {{smaller block|Now, Maria, here is a character ''to'' your taste. {{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|It was a most difficult matter to keep the tunnel ''to'' grade. {{right|''Sci. Amer.'', N. S., LXIV. 52.}}}} 10. In accompaniment with: as, she sang ''to'' his guitar. {{smaller block|They move
In perfect phalanx ''to'' the Dorian mood
Of flutes and soft recorders. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 550.}}}} {{smaller block|Let us but practise a while; and then you shall see me dance the whole Dance ''to'' the Violin. {{right|''Wycherley'', Gentleman Dancing-Master, iv. 1.}}}} 11. In the character, quality, or shape of; for; as. {{smaller block|And Floriz he maketh stonde upriȝt
And ther he dubbede him ''to'' kniȝt. {{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 73.}}}} {{smaller block|He badde me wite of yow what he shulde haue ''to'' rewarde. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 72.}}}} {{smaller block|He hath a pretty young man ''to'' his son, whose name is Civility. {{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim's Progress, i.}}}} {{smaller block|He took a morsel of early lamb ''to'' his dinner. {{right|''Trollope'', Last Chronicle of Barset, xlix.}}}} 12. Regarding; concerning; as to: denoting relation: as, to plead ''to'' the charge; to speak ''to'' the question. {{smaller block|Where we may leisurely Each one demand and answer ''to'' his part Perform'd in this wide gap of time. {{right|''Shak.'', W. T., v. 3. 153.}}}} {{smaller block|It takes away my faith ''to'' anything He shall hereafter speak. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Sejanus, iii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|At these meetings, any of the members of the churches may come, if they please, and speak their minds freely, in the fear of God, ''to'' any matter. {{right|''Penn'', Rise and Progress of Quakers, iv.}}}} {{smaller block|[Dr.] ''To'' a lady's lounging-chair . . . in ebonized wood....................................£ 16-16-0 ''To'' a gentleman's Etruscan do. do., cabriole legs.................................... 17-17-0 {{right|''Miss Braddon'', Hostages of Fortune, p. 115.}}}} 13. Denoting application or attention: as, he fell ''to'' work. {{smaller block|Sing me now asleep; Then ''to'' your offices, and let me rest. {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., ii. 2. 7.}}}} {{smaller block|They begin with porridge, then they fall ''to'' capon, or so forth. ''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, i. 1.}} {{smaller block|The bride and her party, having arrived at the bridegroom's house, sit down ''to'' a repast. {{right|''E. W. Lane'', Modern Egyptians, I. 210.}}}} 14. In connection with; appurtenant: denoting attribution, appurtenance, or belonging: as, a cap with a tassel ''to'' it.
